lesson.title: From Protest to Army: The Second Continental Congress
lesson.summary: Meeting in Philadelphia just weeks after the fighting at Lexington and Concord, the Second Continental Congress created the Continental Army and gradually took on the role of a national government.
lesson.body:
The First Continental Congress had agreed to reconvene in May 1775 if colonial grievances were not resolved, and the outbreak of fighting at Lexington and Concord that April made the meeting urgent rather than optional. Delegates gathered in Philadelphia on May 10, 1775, at the Pennsylvania State House, the building later known as Independence Hall, to decide how the colonies should respond to a war that had already begun without any formal declaration.

The delegates faced an immediate practical problem. Thousands of New England militia had surrounded British forces in Boston, but this collection of local units had no unified command, no central supply system, and no legal standing as an army. On June 14, 1775, Congress voted to create the Continental Army out of these forces, and the next day it selected George Washington of Virginia as commander in chief. Choosing a Virginian to lead what had begun as a Massachusetts fight was a deliberate act of political unity, tying the southern colonies to a conflict that had so far been concentrated in New England.

Even as it built an army, Congress had not yet embraced independence. Many delegates still hoped for reconciliation with Britain, and in July 1775 Congress approved both a Declaration of the Causes and Necessity of Taking Up Arms, explaining why the colonies had armed themselves, and the Olive Branch Petition, a direct appeal to King George III asking him to intervene with Parliament and prevent further bloodshed. The king refused even to receive the petition, and in August he formally declared the colonies to be in a state of rebellion, closing off the path to a peaceful settlement that many moderates had still hoped for.

Over the following months, as fighting spread and British policy hardened, opinion inside Congress shifted steadily toward independence. Congress authorized privateers to attack British shipping, opened American ports to trade with nations other than Britain, and began encouraging individual colonies to write new state constitutions, all steps that made sense only if the colonies intended to govern themselves permanently rather than simply negotiate better terms within the empire.

By the spring of 1776, with public opinion further galvanized by Thomas Paine's pamphlet Common Sense, Congress moved toward a final break. In June 1776 it appointed a committee, including Thomas Jefferson, to draft a formal declaration, and on July 4, 1776, it adopted the Declaration of Independence. What had begun as a meeting to coordinate resistance had become, in little more than a year, the government of a new nation at war.

Benjamin Franklin, who returned from years in London just as the Congress convened, brought both diplomatic experience and a reputation across Europe that would later prove valuable in winning French support for the American cause. By the time Congress turned to drafting a declaration of independence in the summer of 1776, it had already been functioning as the de facto government of a country at war for more than a year.
